title: APPLICATION OF DEEP QUANTUM NEURAL NETWORKS TO FINANCE
abstract_summary: This preprint investigates the application of deep quantum neural networks (DQNNs) to finance, demonstrating simple experiments in learning implied volatility surfaces and option prices. It shows that Greeks such as delta and gamma can be computed analytically from the learned DQNN, presents numerical results that indicate promise for financial numerical problems, and discusses practical implementation challenges (e.g. SWAP/partial-trace requirements and barren-plateau issues) on near-term quantum devices.
methodology_description: The paper implements and evaluates the Deep Quantum Neural Network (DQNN) architecture of Beer et al. (2020) on small-scale financial learning tasks (learning implied volatilities; learning option prices and Greeks). Financial scalar inputs are encoded into single-qubit pure states via a sigmoid-to-Bloch mapping P(s,t,u) (eq. 11) and corresponding density matrices. The DQNN is built with an input layer, one hidden layer, and an output layer; feedforward is modeled via successive CPTP channels (Kraus representation) implemented by parameterized unitaries acting on the layer qubits plus ancilla |0...0⟩ qubits, followed by partial trace of the preceding layer. Training maximizes an average fidelity-based cost (eq. 5) between predicted and target output states; for the Greeks experiment the cost is augmented by fidelity terms between target and predicted first/second derivative density matrices (weighted by νd and νg). Parameter updates are performed classically using the analytic K-matrix gradient approximation derived in Beer et al., updating each unitary as U ← exp(i K ϵ) U with K computed from layer-wise forward and adjoint states (equations (9)-(10) and their differential extensions). Experiments are run in a MATLAB-based DQNN simulator (public code referenced by the authors). Hyperparameters and network topologies are varied (e.g., hidden-qubit counts, β and γ encoding scalars, µ scaling for derivative states, νd/νg weights, η/ϵ learning step sizing), and performance is reported as output fidelity and direct numeric comparisons between predicted and training implied volatilities, option prices, deltas and gammas.
algorithms_used: Classical gradient-based parameter update via K-matrix (U -> exp(i K epsilon) U)
experimental_setup: Simulation using publicly available MATLAB DQNN code (GitHub link provided in paper). No quantum hardware (QPU) used; experiments run on the MATLAB simulator implementation of the DQNN.
dataset_used: Two data sources: (1) Market implied volatility data referenced from Antonov et al. (2015) used for implied-volatility learning (seven strikes reported in tables). (2) Synthetic Black–Scholes-generated training sets for option price and Greeks: seven tuples (spot x, call price V, delta, gamma) computed under Black–Scholes (K=100, r=0.0, T=0.25, vol=0.15).
experiment_input: Implied vol experiment: market strikes (seven strike points) and corresponding implied vols from Antonov et al. (2015); values encoded to single-qubit states via φ_in = cos(P(F,K,β))|0> + sin(P(F,K,β))|1>, φ_out = cos(P(σ_K,K,γ))|0> + sin(P(σ_K,K,γ))|1>. Option/Greeks experiment: seven training tuples sampled under Black–Scholes (K=100,r=0.0,T=0.25,σ=0.15). Encoding similar: input encodes asset x with parameter β, output encodes price V with parameter γ. Preprocessing consists of applying the sigmoid mapping P(s,t,u) to scale numeric values into Bloch-sphere angles; for Greeks the derivatives dρ_in/dx and scaled quantum states dρ_in,m/dx are formed using scaling µ parameters to ensure valid density matrices.
experiment_process: 1) Encode scalar inputs and targets into single-qubit states via P(s,t,u) mapping and construct density matrices. 2) Build DQNN with specified topology (input qubit(s), one hidden layer with m1 qubits, output qubit), implement feedforward as tensorization with |0...0> ancilla, apply layer unitaries and partial trace to obtain predicted output density matrix ρ_out^D. 3) For Greeks: compute analytic dρ_in/dx (and second derivative), convert to valid density matrices by scaling (µ) and add to training set; augment cost with fidelity terms for these derivative states weighted by νd and νg. 4) Compute layer-wise forward states ρ_l and backward adjoint states σ_l (adjoint channel) and assemble the K-matrix using the formulas given (equations (9)-(10) and their differential extensions). 5) Update unitaries using U ← exp(i K ϵ) U. 6) Repeat updates for a fixed number of iterations and monitor fidelity C and numeric prediction errors. Parameters used in reported runs: input/output qubits = 1, hidden layer qubits typically 2 or 3, L=1; learning rate(s) η (named λ in some text) = 1, step size ϵ = 0.1, iterations = 800, seed = 0; encoding β and γ varied per experiment; µin = µout = 2 for Greeks experiments; νd and νg varied (0, 0.01, 0.05 etc.).
experiment_output: Outputs reported as fidelity C (average output fidelity across training pairs) and tables of predicted vs training numeric values: implied volatilities (in bps) per strike with absolute differences; predicted option prices, deltas, and gammas for a range of spot prices, reported side-by-side with training (Black–Scholes) values. No explicit external baseline algorithms (e.g., classical neural net baseline) are reported; evaluation is by fidelity and direct numeric error (difference columns in tables).

key_findings: [supported] The Deep Quantum Neural Network (DQNN) architecture of Beer et al. (2020) can be adapted to finance tasks such as learning implied volatilities and option prices (demonstrated in numerical simulations).

[supported] In simulated experiments on small datasets, the DQNN achieved high fidelity values when learning implied volatilities (reported C ≈ 0.9984–0.9999) with per-strike absolute errors reported in the paper's tables.

[supported] The DQNN can be used to produce analytic expressions for Greeks (delta and gamma) via derivatives of density-matrix outputs, and these were evaluated in the paper's simulation experiments (results reported for a seven-sample Black–Scholes dataset).

[speculative] The author claims the DQNN is a promising and potentially efficient technique for solving numerical problems in finance (general potential claimed but not demonstrated on quantum hardware or large datasets).
[speculative] The DQNN may be robust to NISQ noise as suggested by Beer et al. (2020), but robustness on real financial workloads or hardware was not empirically demonstrated in this work.

[supported] Practical implementation on quantum hardware would require efficient SWAP gates and partial-trace operations; current implementation details and hardware suitability remain open practical challenges (not solved here).

[supported] The paper acknowledges the barren plateau problem for quantum neural networks (citing McClean et al. (2018) and Sharma (2020)) and notes DQNNs are vulnerable to the same issue, implying careful circuit design is needed.

[speculative] Arbitrage-free constraints (e.g., monotonicity and convexity in strikes, time monotonicity) can be incorporated into the DQNN training via penalties, but this requires accurate and efficient estimation of Greeks and was not implemented here.
results_summary: This preprint adapts the Deep Quantum Neural Network (DQNN) framework to two finance tasks and reports results from classical simulations. First, the author maps strike and volatility data into single-qubit states and demonstrates that small DQNNs (one input qubit, one output qubit, one hidden layer of 2–3 qubits) can learn implied volatilities with high fidelity (C ≈ 0.998–0.9999) and modest per-strike errors. Second, the paper shows how option prices and their Greeks (delta, gamma) can be represented and learned by the DQNN; analytic expressions link density-matrix outputs to Greeks, and the author reports simulated prediction results on a seven-sample Black–Scholes dataset. The work is simulation-based and highlights implementation challenges (hardware requirements, barren-plateau training issues) and the need for larger-scale studies on actual quantum devices.
performance_claims: Implied volatility learning experiments (simulation): reported fidelity values C = 0.9984 (β=1.0, γ=1.0), C = 0.9998 (β=0.5, γ=0.5), C = 0.9997 (β=0.25, γ=0.25), and C = 0.9999 (β=0.25, γ=0.25, hidden layer size m1=3). Per-strike absolute errors reported in Tables 1–4 (examples: for strike 0.06% training σ=23.5 bps, outputs ranged 21.1–21.9 bps; for strike 2.56% training σ=140.5 bps, outputs ranged 132.6–137.5 bps).

Option pricing + Greeks experiment (simulation, Black–Scholes with K=100, r=0, T=0.25, vol=0.15): seven training samples. Predicted call prices varied modestly from training values (e.g., training price at x=100: 2.991; predicted 2.990–3.001 under various νd/νg settings). Predicted deltas and gammas are reported in Tables 6–7 with deviations from training values (examples: training delta at x=100 = 0.515, predicted 0.485–0.488; training gamma at x=100 = 0.0532, predicted 0.0469–0.0482).
Training parameters in simulations: one hidden layer with m1 in {2,3}, learning rate λ=1, step ǫ=0.1, 800 update iterations, µin=µout=2 for Greeks experiments.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper suggests DQNNs are a promising approach and references potential robustness to NISQ noise (from Beer et al.) but does not demonstrate any algorithmic or runtime quantum advantage for finance tasks. All presented results are classical simulations of DQNNs on very small datasets; no speed-up, scaling advantage, or hardware-based advantage is shown. Thus any claim of quantum advantage remains speculative and unproven in this work.
limitations: Numerical experiments are simple and small-scale (learning implied volatilities and option prices with very small networks and datasets).

Implementation on real quantum hardware requires quantum computers with high capacity (efficient SWAP gates and partial trace operations), which may not be available: 'we would need a quantum computer with high capacity...'.
Arbitrage-free conditions for implied volatility surfaces were not enforced in the experiments.
Time-to-maturity was fixed in the implied volatility experiments (limiting extension to full volatility surfaces unless modified).
DQNNs are subject to the barren plateau problem (vanishing gradients) which requires careful network construction: 'this issue arises in QNNs... and the DQNN is no exception'.
Trade-off between memory savings and multiple network evaluations: reducing memory requires more evaluations (could impact run time on NISQs).

#idea:hybrid-approach — Encodes scalar financial inputs/targets (spot, implied vol, option price) into single-qubit pure states via a sigmoid-to-Bloch mapping and uses density-matrix CPTP-layer feedforward with ancilla and partial trace.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrates that Greeks (delta, gamma) can be computed analytically from the learned DQNN by forming scaled derivative density matrices and augmenting the fidelity-based cost, showing promising numeric fidelity on small simulated datasets.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Reports practical implementation challenges for NISQ devices (SWAP/partial-trace overheads, ancilla/qubit requirements, barren-plateau training issues) and discusses their impact on near-term feasibility.
